learning: If oscillation falls below 0.28 with progress held near 0.47, the next step is a small mass increase or a track of 0.12 m. If progress falls, return to 0.10 m and treat excursions with controller damping instead of geometry.
notes: Single-variable test of wheel_track (0.11 m) against iteration 1. The controller is unchanged, so the race isolates the geometry effect. Lower effective gain from the wider track is accepted as part of the test.
rationale: Evidence: iteration 1 (wheel_track 0.10, lead 0.03 m, kp 2.5, kd 0.30) is the best measured design at 114.4, with oval progress 0.47 and oval steering_oscillation 0.28. Every run ends off track with max_error 0.061 to 0.068 m, just above the 0.06 m floor, while rms_error stays at 0.023 to 0.031 m. Sensor changes (iterations 2, 3, 5, 6) did not beat iteration 1: the 0.02 m lead gave 91.8 with s-bend progress 0.11, and the 0.04 m lead gave 109.9 with s-bend progress 0.246 against 0.256 at 0.03 m. Iteration 4 showed that a faster, lighter drivetrain raises oscillation to 0.33 without gaining progress. The wheel_track lever has not been isolated. Iteration 7 changes only wheel_track, from 0.10 to 0.11 m, which lowers yaw rate per wheel differential by about 9 percent. Decision: keep the iteration-1 controller exactly (base_speed 1.5, kp 2.5, ki 0, kd 0.30, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2], last_direction). I considered raising kp to 2.75 to hold the effective gain constant, but that would confound the single-variable test the Builder asked for, so I leave it unchanged and let the race show whether the lower effective gain damps the oscillation. Expected: oscillation below 0.28, max_error near or below 0.06 m, oval progress near 0.47. Risk: lower turn authority may lose progress on the slalom and tightest bends.
